chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: The Benjamin Harrison Literary Club
summary: How the downtown club got its name, became a speak-easy after the Volstead Act, and drew mixed crowds after work.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Do you know how it got that name?

Well, it was supposed to have been a charter club, you know. There's a possibility at one time it was a literary club. Benjamin Harrison was one of our Presidents. So it probably was a legitimate club at one time. It was a chartered club. And it had a membership. Of course by 1936, you know, when I got in there, it was not the literary club that it might have been in the early days. It was an old club, definitely chartered. Because, you know --
And then it became a speak-easy.

It became a speak-easy I imagine when the amendment --

Yeah, the town went dry. It was right downtown in Pittsburgh. It was a very popular spot. What I wanted to say was, you see, in Pittsburgh at repeal, the legitimate houses that sold liquor and beer had to close at 2 o'clock in the morning. Wherein before repeal these clubs probably were operating illegitimately, but because the early closing in Pittsburgh, people would want to find some place else to go. So a lot of people started digging up charters and a lot of clubs opened up as charter clubs. Because the legitimate places had to close at 2:00. Before repeal they may have stayed open all night. But because of the new law they had to close at 2:00, so they started digging up charters and they found these old -- there was a story about the Benjamin Harrison Literary Club later, they got into some kind of trouble, I don't know, this was later, long after I had left Pittsburgh. And it seems that one of the owners or operators was before the Judge and the Judge

asked -- he said it was the Benjamin Harrison Literary Club -- the Judge asked him if he had anything in there by Voltaire and the guy said, "No, what did that cat play?" (Laughter) But I think that was just a joke. But the Benjamin Harrison Literary Club was quite popular and most of the musicians who came to Pittsburgh to play --

White and Black would line up there after work because they had a very good chef there and they would come there to eat and then they had to listen to me and Jenny. It was just piano and vocal. And of course I sang at tables then. The club had eight tables in it. I think that was the first club that I could stand in the middle of the floor and sing and everybody could hear me. But that was my first BIG opportunity, I mean, I really said, well, I'm really in now. Because I saved my money and the next step is New York. And by this time I'd been listening to Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday, most of the pop singers and the bands.
